<script>
  // Restore the saved color scheme preference, or
  // enact the browser preference if "automatic", 
  // without expecting DOM load to have completed.
  //
  // Also restore any saved readingmode and ToC display preferences.
  function initializeReadingPreferences() {
    let saved_theme = localStorage.getItem("ar5iv_theme") || "automatic";
    if (saved_theme === "automatic") {
      if (window.matchMedia("(prefers-color-scheme: dark)").matches) {
        saved_theme = "dark";
      }
    }
    if (saved_theme == "dark") {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "dark");
    } else {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-theme", "light");
    }

    const tocDisplay = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_toc_display');
    if (tocDisplay) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-toc-display", tocDisplay);
    }
    const readingMode = localStorage.getItem('arxiv_html_paper_reading_mode');
    if (readingMode) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-reading-mode", readingMode);
    }
    // Pre-apply spinout-banner dismissal here, before the banner paints, so it
    // never flashes in only to be hidden later by the deferred arxiv-header.js.
    // Key matches arxiv-header.js: "arxiv-banner-dismissed:" + data-banner-name.
    if (localStorage.getItem('arxiv-banner-dismissed:spinout-nonprofit')) {
      document.documentElement.setAttribute("data-banner-dismissed", "");
    }
  }
  // Run as soon as JS starts, to minimize repainting
  initializeReadingPreferences();
</script>

</ol></li>
</ol></li>

<div id="abstract1" class="ltx_abstract"><h6 class="ltx_title ltx_title_abstract">Abstract</h6>
    
<p id="abstract1.1" class="ltx_p">Theory of Mind (ToM) is the cognitive capability to perceive and ascribe mental states to oneself and others. Recent research has sparked a debate over whether large language models (LLMs) exhibit a form of ToM. However, existing ToM evaluations are hindered by challenges such as constrained scope, subjective judgment, and unintended contamination, yielding inadequate assessments. To address this gap, we introduce <span id="abstract1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="abstract1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span> with three key characteristics: a systematic evaluation framework encompassing 8 tasks and 31 abilities in social cognition, a multiple-choice question format to support automated and unbiased evaluation, and a build-from-scratch bilingual inventory to strictly avoid data leakage.
Based on <span id="abstract1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="abstract1.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span>, we conduct extensive experiments to evaluate the ToM performance of 10 popular LLMs across tasks and abilities. We find that even the most advanced LLMs like GPT-4 lag behind human performance by over 10% points, indicating that LLMs have not achieved a human-level theory of mind yet.
Our aim with <span id="abstract1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="abstract1.g3" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span> is to enable an efficient and effective evaluation of LLMs’ ToM capabilities, thereby facilitating the development of LLMs with inherent social intelligence.</p>
  
</div>
<div id="p1" class="ltx_para ltx_align_bottom">
<p id="p1.1" class="ltx_p ltx_align_center" style="width:345.0pt;"><span id="p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_inline-block" style="width:0.0pt;">
</span></p>
</div>
<section id="S1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">1 </span>Introduction</h2>

<div id="S1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Theory of Mind (ToM) is a fundamental psychological process, involving the capability to attribute mental states – beliefs, intents, desires, emotions, knowledge, etc. – to oneself and others <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib53" title="" class="ltx_ref">Premack and Woodruff (1978)</a></cite>.
ToM is essential for human social cognition <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Baron-Cohen et al. (1985)</a></cite> and plays an important role in social activities like empathetic communication <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib19" title="" class="ltx_ref">Decety and Jackson (2004)</a></cite>, relationship maintenance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib60" title="" class="ltx_ref">Slaughter et al. (2002)</a></cite>, decision making <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib16" title="" class="ltx_ref">Carlson and Moses (2001)</a></cite>, and childhood education <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib15" title="" class="ltx_ref">Caputi et al. (2012)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">With the advent of the era of large language models (LLMs), powerful LLMs like GPT-4 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Achiam et al. (2023)</a></cite> and LLaMA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">Touvron et al. (2023)</a></cite> have demonstrated comparable performance to humans in solving tasks. Consequently, researchers have grown increasingly curious that “<span id="S1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Do large language models have a theory of mind?</span>”, while the subsequent assessments have yielded inconsistent and even contradictory results. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kosinski (2023)</a></cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bubeck et al. (2023)</a></cite> find that GPT-3.5/4 achieve remarkably high performance on the false belief task <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wimmer and Perner (1983)</a></cite>, suggesting that ToM may have spontaneously emerged in LLMs. However, later studies reveal that LLMs’ ToM performance dramatically decreases when faced with trivial alterations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ullman (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shapira et al. (2023)</a></cite>. This suggests a phenomenon called “Clever Hans” <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib38" title="" class="ltx_ref">Lapuschkin et al. (2019)</a></cite> denoting that LLMs rely on unexpected spurious correlations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib59" title="" class="ltx_ref">Simon and Simon (1977)</a></cite> rather than truly possessing a “Mind Reading” ability.
This ongoing debate underscores the pressing need for a holistic ToM benchmark.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F1" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2402.15052v1/introduction.png" id="S1.F1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:452/172;" width="452" height="172" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 1: </span><span id="S1.F1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="S1.F1.g4" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="Refer to caption">MBench</span> is a systematic, automated, and original bilingual ToM benchmark for LLMs, covering 8 tasks and 31 abilities. <span id="S1.F1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="S1.F1.g5" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="Refer to caption">MBench</span> contains 2,860 testing samples involving diverse real-world social scenarios.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Despite its critical importance, the development of such a benchmark still faces three major challenges.
<span id="S1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">1) Constrained scope</span>. Existing studies mainly evaluate LLMs on specific ToM dimensions like emotions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sap et al. (2019)</a></cite> and beliefs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib72" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al. (2023)</a></cite>. While inspiring, they fall short of providing a complete ToM assessment.
<span id="S1.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">2) Subjective judgment</span>. Most existing inventories for ToM evaluation involve open-ended questions where responses require manual scoring by experts <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Beaudoin et al. (2020)</a></cite>.
While this approach works on small-scale and focused ToM tests for children, it is impractical for benchmarking due to the high annotation cost required for comprehensively evaluating LLMs. Additionally, human evaluations towards diverse answers may introduce potential inconsistency and bias <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib34" title="" class="ltx_ref">Klie et al. (2023)</a></cite>.
<span id="S1.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">3) Unintended contamination</span>. Although merely combining different inventories can create a corpus involving multiple ToM aspects, it is still not qualified for being a benchmark. Since most ToM inventories in psychology research are released far before the launch of LLMs,
they are likely to have appeared in the training process of LLMs, whether during pre-training, SFT, or RLHF <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Golchin and Surdeanu (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li and Flanigan (2023)</a></cite>. We present a simple verification in Appendix <a href="#A1" title="Appendix A Inventory Contamination in LLMs ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">A</span></a>. The potential contamination indicates a risk that LLMs might complete ToM evaluations in an “open-book” status, leading to inflated performance <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shapira et al. (2023)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p4.1" class="ltx_p">To address the above challenges, we propose <span id="S1.p4.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="S1.p4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span>, a ToM benchmark for LLMs featuring three key characteristics.
<span id="S1.p4.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">1) Systematic framework</span>. We first review broad psychological literature and identify 8 well-defined theory-of-mind tasks in <span id="S1.p4.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="S1.p4.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span>. Then, since tasks are the means and abilities are the core, we further ground <span id="S1.p4.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="S1.p4.g3" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span> in a well-structured psychological framework, ATOMS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Beaudoin et al. (2020)</a></cite>, expanding our evaluation to encompass 31 core theory-of-mind abilities. We hereby design both task- and ability-oriented evaluations to comprehensively assess the ToM capabilities of LLMs.
<span id="S1.p4.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">2) Multi-choice question format</span>.
We define every test sample in <span id="S1.p4.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="S1.p4.g4" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span> as a story, followed by a question, and several plausible options where only one answer is correct and the others are high-quality but misleading wrong answers. This multiple-choice question (MCQ) format enables automated and efficient evaluation, avoiding the high labor costs and potential inconsistencies in manual scoring.
<span id="S1.p4.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">3) Build-from-scratch inventory</span>. We do not use any existing inventories. Instead, after being trained by professional psychologists who are proficient in ToM, we authors draw inspiration from daily social scenarios and manually create 2,860 original test samples, each available in both Chinese and English.
We also implement strict annotation and validation procedures to ensure the data quality.
The resulting inventory includes the above-mentioned 8 tasks and 31 abilities for ToM evaluation, covering a wide range of real-world human social scenarios across diverse topics.</p>
</div>
<div id="S1.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p5.1" class="ltx_p">Using <span id="S1.p5.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="S1.p5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span>, we conduct both task- and ability-oriented evaluations of 10 popular LLMs with vanilla and CoT prompting. We also recruit 20 graduate students to provide an expected human baseline ToM performance. The experimental results show that, the GPT-4 series outperforms other LLMs across ToM tasks and abilities, yet their average performance is significantly lower than human levels by over 10% points.
Further analysis shows that when facing a more rigorous and comprehensive understanding of social scenarios, the gap in ToM performance between LLMs and humans widens. Moreover, inspecting the internal attention of LLMs reveals their decision-making processes notably differ from those of humans.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S1.F2" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2402.15052v1/atoms.svg" id="S1.F2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:476/206;" width="476" height="206"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 2: </span>The mapping between 8 tasks and 31 ATOMS abilities. The suffix after each ability indicates its occurrence within specific tasks, whereas those with “#” are not covered by tasks and are evaluated with extra test samples.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S1.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S1.p6.1" class="ltx_p">To the best of our knowledge, <span id="S1.p6.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="S1.p6.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span> is the first systematic ToM benchmark for automated ToM evaluation of LLMs.
We hope that <span id="S1.p6.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="S1.p6.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span> will drive construction through evaluation, facilitating the development of LLMs in the realm of social intelligence, thereby complementing their task-solving capabilities. A broader objective is to enable LLMs to transcend the superficial layer of natural language and delve deeper into understanding the mental states and cognitive processes behind human words,
hereby foster more efficient and seamless human-AI interaction. We will release the code and data of <span id="S1.p6.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="S1.p6.g3" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span> at <a href="https://%7Bhttps://github.com/zhchen18/ToMBench%7D" title="" class="ltx_ref ltx_url ltx_font_typewriter">{https://github.com/zhchen18/ToMBench}</a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">2 </span><span id="S2.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="S2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span> Framework</h2>

<section id="S2.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.1 </span>8 Theory-of-Mind Tasks</h3>

<div id="S2.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The essence of the theory of mind is <span id="S2.SS1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">social understanding</span>, which refers to the ability of humans to perceive and ascribe mental states to themselves and others in social scenarios. In <span id="S2.SS1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="S2.SS1.p1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span>, we first identify 8 social cognitive tasks that have been widely proven in psychology to effectively assess ToM capabilities: <span id="S2.SS1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Unexpected Outcome Test</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dyck et al. (2001)</a></cite>, <span id="S2.SS1.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Scalar Implicature Task</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Goodman and Stuhlmüller (2013)</a></cite>, <span id="S2.SS1.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Persuasion Story Task</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kołodziejczyk and Bosacki (2016)</a></cite>, <span id="S2.SS1.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">False Belief Task</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wimmer and Perner (1983)</a></cite>, <span id="S2.SS1.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ambiguous Story Task</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bosacki and Wilde Astington (1999)</a></cite>, <span id="S2.SS1.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Hinting Test</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Corcoran et al. (1995)</a></cite>, <span id="S2.SS1.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Strange Story Task</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Happé (1994)</a></cite>, <span id="S2.SS1.p1.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Faux-pas Recognition Test</span> <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Baron-Cohen et al. (1999)</a></cite>. We then construct test samples for these tasks based on definitions, descriptions, and examples in the original psychology literature.
Due to space constraints, we present the details of all tasks in Appendix <a href="#A2" title="Appendix B Details of Theory-of-Mind Tasks ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">B</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S2.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">2.2 </span>31 Theory-of-Mind Abilities</h3>

<div id="S2.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Drawing from expertise in psychology, we gain insight into the principle that tasks are means, while abilities are the core <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib54" title="" class="ltx_ref">Quesque and Rossetti (2020)</a></cite>.
Thus, we further resort to a well-defined psychological framework, “Abilities in the Theory-of-Mind Space (ATOMS)” <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Beaudoin et al. (2020)</a></cite>.
Originally designed for an extensive analysis of psychological ToM measures towards young children, ATOMS outlines 7 distinct ability dimensions: <span id="S2.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Emotion</span>, <span id="S2.SS2.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Desire</span>, <span id="S2.SS2.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Intention</span>, <span id="S2.SS2.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Percept</span>, <span id="S2.SS2.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Knowledge</span>, <span id="S2.SS2.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Belief</span>, and <span id="S2.SS2.p1.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Non-literal Communication</span>, embracing 39 specific theory-of-mind abilities. After removing the <span id="S2.SS2.p1.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Percept</span> dimension requiring visual cues and some mixed abilities, we retain a total of 6 dimensions and 31 abilities in <span id="S2.SS2.p1.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="S2.SS2.p1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">However, as shown in Figure <a href="#S1.F2" title="Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>,
the above-mentioned 8 tasks only encompass 19/31 abilities in ATOMS.
Therefore, to address the remaining 12 abilities, we again refer back to the original literature to supplement extra ability-specific test samples, thereby extending the evaluation scope of <span id="S2.SS2.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="S2.SS2.p2.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span> to a complete set of 31 abilities. Due to space limitation, we here briefly introduce 6 ability dimensions, while the complete details of 31 specific abilities can be found in Appendix <a href="#A3" title="Appendix C Details of Theory-of-Mind Abilities ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">C</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<div id="S2.SS2.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S2.SS2.p3.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="S2.SS2.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">1) Emotion</span> involves <span id="S2.SS2.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">7</span> abilities to understand that situational factors influence people’s emotional states, that people can experience complex emotions, and that people can regulate emotional expressions. <span id="S2.SS2.p3.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">2) Desire</span> involves <span id="S2.SS2.p3.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">4</span> abilities to understand that people have subjective desires, preferences, and wants that influence their emotions and actions. <span id="S2.SS2.p3.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">3) Intention</span> involves <span id="S2.SS2.p3.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">4</span> abilities to understand that people undertake actions in pursuit of goals and intentions. <span id="S2.SS2.p3.1.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">4) Knowledge</span> involves <span id="S2.SS2.p3.1.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">4</span> abilities to understand that others have access to different knowledge based on their perceptions, information they have received, or familiarity with things. <span id="S2.SS2.p3.1.9" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">5) Belief</span> involves <span id="S2.SS2.p3.1.10" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">6</span> abilities to understand that people can hold beliefs about the world that are different from reality or different from one’s own beliefs. <span id="S2.SS2.p3.1.11" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">6) Non-literal Communication</span> involves <span id="S2.SS2.p3.1.12" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">6</span> abilities to understand that communication can convey meaning beyond the literal words spoken.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">3 </span><span id="S3.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="S3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span> Construction</h2>

<section id="S3.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.1 </span>Overview</h3>

<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Principles</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We authors act as workers and build <span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px1.p1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span> from scratch. We do not use any existing inventories from psychological literature due to the potential risk of data contamination and the limited size of test samples. To ensure the effectiveness of inventory, all workers have undergone training by psychology experts, gaining a solid understanding of ToM. Furthermore, all workers have thoroughly reviewed the related psychology literature, adhering strictly to the specific definitions, descriptions, and examples of tasks and abilities.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.F3" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2402.15052v1/pie.svg" id="S3.F3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:272/192;" width="272" height="192"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 3: </span>Topics of social scenarios in <span id="S3.F3.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="S3.F3.g3" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="Refer to caption">MBench</span>. Under 9 primary topics, we highlight the top-5 sub-topics with the highest frequency.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Procedure</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We first craft samples for 8 tasks, with each worker responsible for at least one, covering 19 abilities in total. Owing to the natural difficulty of tasks and abilities, we ensure that each task has <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\geq" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>≥</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\geq</annotation></semantics></math>100 samples, and each ability within a task has <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\geq" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>≥</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\geq</annotation></semantics></math>20 samples. This step results in the creation of 2,470 samples. Subsequently, we add extra samples for the remaining 12 abilities not previously covered, with <math id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px2.p1.m3" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\geq" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>≥</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\geq</annotation></semantics></math>20 samples for each ability, bringing the total number of samples to 2,860.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Statistics</h4>

<div id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In Table <a href="#S3.T1" title="Table 1 ‣ Statistics ‣ 3.1 Overview ‣ 3 TMBench Construction ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">1</span></a>, we present the data statistics of <span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span>. Due to space constraints, the detailed statistics of the 31 abilities are present in Appendix <a href="#A4" title="Appendix D Detailed Data Statistics ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">D</span></a>.
As shown in Figure <a href="#S3.F3" title="Figure 3 ‣ Principles ‣ 3.1 Overview ‣ 3 TMBench Construction ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, <span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span> includes diverse daily topics, such as <span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">school</span>, <span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">workplace</span>, <span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">family</span>, <span id="S3.SS1.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">neighborhood</span>, etc. These real-life social scenarios are crucial for an effective ToM evaluation, just as we mentioned earlier, the essence of the theory of mind is social understanding.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S3.T1" class="ltx_table">
<div id="S3.T1.2" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_transformed_outer" style="width:148.3pt;height:113.8pt;vertical-align:-55.6pt;"><span class="ltx_transformed_inner" style="transform:translate(-68.2pt,52.3pt) scale(0.52092310997864,0.52092310997864) ;">
<table id="S3.T1.2.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="S3.T1.2.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S3.T1.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_r ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:1.4pt;padding-right:1.4pt;"></td>
<td id="S3.T1.2.1.1.2" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:1.4pt;padding-right:1.4pt;"><span id="S3.T1.2.1.1.2.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">#S</span></td>
<td id="S3.T1.2.1.1.3" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:1.4pt;padding-right:1.4pt;"><span id="S3.T1.2.1.1.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">#Q</span></td>
<td id="S3.T1.2.1.1.4" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left ltx_border_tt" style="padding-left:1.4pt;padding-right:1.4pt;"><span id="S3.T1.2.1.1.4.1" class="ltx_text"></span> <span id="S3.T1.2.1.1.4.2" class="ltx_text">
<span id="S3.T1.2.1.1.4.2.1" class="ltx_tabular ltx_align_middle">
<span id="S3.T1.2.1.1.4.2.1.1" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S3.T1.2.1.1.4.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center" style="padding-left:1.4pt;padding-right:1.4pt;"><span id="S3.T1.2.1.1.4.2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ASL</span></span></span>
<span id="S3.T1.2.1.1.4.2.1.2" class="ltx_tr">
<span id="S3.T1.2.1.1.4.2.1.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_center" style="padding-left:1.4pt;padding-right:1.4pt;"><span id="S3.T1.2.1.1.4.2.1.2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">(En)</span></span></span>

<td id="S3.T1.2.1.17.5" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:1.4pt;padding-right:1.4pt;">143.91</td>
<td id="S3.T1.2.1.17.6" class="ltx_td ltx_nopad_l ltx_nopad_r ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb" style="padding-left:1.4pt;padding-right:1.4pt;">99.4%</td></tr>
</table>
</span></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 1: </span>Data statistics. #S: Number of stories, #Q: Number of questions, ASL(En/Zh): Average story length (English/Chinese). Agr.: Final agreement.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.2 </span>Data Collection</h3>

<div id="S3.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We here detail the process of data collection. We construct <span id="S3.SS2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="S3.SS2.p1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span> in the form of multiple-choice questions to avoid the high costs of manual scoring, and ensure an unbiased and consistent evaluation. Each sample is defined as a combination of a story, a question, and several options.</p>
</div>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Story</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">describes a scenario from everyday life, including characters’ actions and interactions, to set the context for evaluation. The inspiration for stories primarily comes from posts on social platforms like Reddit, Twitter, Zhihu, and Weibo, such as “<span id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">What kind of hints have you understood from others</span>?” The design of stories refers to the setting in psychology literature while ensuring variety in social scenarios.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Question</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">asks subjects to understand specific aspects of the story, which strictly adheres to psychological definitions of ToM tasks and abilities. Every question is designed to be answerable by humans. A story can correspond to multiple questions, each exploring different aspects of a social scenario to assess a comprehensive understanding, where each question represents a unique test sample.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Options</h4>

<div id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">include one correct answer and several misleading incorrect answers. The incorrect options are designed to be plausible, avoiding outliers that are easily dismissed. Options are generally of two types: for true/false questions, such as “Is what PersonA said true?”, the options are simply yes/no. For explanatory questions, such as “Why did PersonB say this?”, there are four options provided.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.3 </span>Data Validation &amp; Translation</h3>

<div id="S3.SS3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">After the data collection, we conduct two rounds of validation to ensure the data quality. In 1st round, worker A would first complete all samples created by worker B. For stories, questions, and options where there are disagreements, workers A and B would discuss and modify them to reach a consensus as much as possible. In 2nd round, for samples where consensus is still not reached, another worker C would discuss with workers A and B to determine the final answer. After two rounds of discussion, the final average agreement reaches 99.4%. The inventory is initially crafted in Chinese. We then carefully use GPT-4-0613 to translate it into English, and manually check all translated samples to support bilingual ToM evaluation. Note that we do not provide correct answers in translation, thus there is no data leakage. The translation prompts can be found in Appendix <a href="#A5" title="Appendix E Prompts for Data Translation ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">E</span></a>. Since we authors act as workers, we do not pay any other individuals for data collection.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 2: </span>Task-oriented ToM performance. The best results of vanilla prompting are in <span id="S3.T2.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#ED6498;">pink</span>, and those of CoT prompting are in <span id="S3.T2.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#007EDB;">blue</span>. “LLM Grand Mean” is the average performance of all ten LLMs (same as below).
</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S3.SS4" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">3.4 </span>Evaluation Method</h3>

<div id="S3.SS4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S3.SS4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In <span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="S3.SS4.p1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span>, we organize the test samples in two perspectives: the task view groups them into 8 theory-of-mind tasks, and the ability view categorizes them into 31 specific theory-of-mind abilities. The former approach is more general and commonly used in psychology research; the latter is more comprehensive, allowing us to inspect the performance of each specific ability. Accordingly, we report both <span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">task-oriented</span> and <span id="S3.SS4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">ability-oriented</span> results by averaging the samples related to a specific task or ability. For evaluation, we present LLMs with a story, a question, and several options, then ask them to pick the correct answer.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">4 </span>Experiments</h2>

<section id="S4.SS1" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.1 </span>Experimental Setup</h3>

<div id="S4.SS1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We evaluate a total of 10 popular LLMs, including GPT-4-1106 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI (2023b)</a></cite>, GPT-4-0613 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib1" title="" class="ltx_ref">Achiam et al. (2023)</a></cite>, GPT-3.5-Turbo-1106 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib47" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI (2023b)</a></cite>, GPT-3.5-Turbo-0613 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib46" title="" class="ltx_ref">OpenAI (2023a)</a></cite>, ChatGLM3-6B <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib64" title="" class="ltx_ref">THUDM (2023)</a></cite>, LLaMA2-13B-Chat <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib65" title="" class="ltx_ref">Touvron et al. (2023)</a></cite>, Baichuan2-13B-Chat <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib5" title="" class="ltx_ref">Baichuan-Inc (2023)</a></cite>, Qwen-14B-Chat <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib4" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bai et al. (2023)</a></cite>, Mistral-7B-v0.2 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib29" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jiang et al. (2023)</a></cite>, and Mixtral-8x7B-Instruct-v0.1 <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib44" title="" class="ltx_ref">Mistral AI (2023)</a></cite>. For GPT* and other open LLMs, we strictly abide by their terms and get access through official APIs and model weights, respectively.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We employ two prompting methods: the <span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">vanilla</span> prompting directly asks LLMs to give a choice, while the <span id="S4.SS1.p2.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">CoT</span> prompting elicits step-by-step reasoning. The prompts are detailed in Appendix <a href="#A6" title="Appendix F Prompts for ToM Evaluation ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">F</span></a>.
For all models (except GPT-4-*), to avoid the bias from option IDs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib73" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zheng et al. (2023)</a></cite>, we shuffle the option orders five times and choose the most frequently selected option as the final answer.
For the GPT-4-* models, our pilot experiments show very consistent answers across different option orders, so we only use the result from one round of answering. Accuracy is used as the metric.</p>
</div>
<div id="S4.SS1.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS1.p3.1" class="ltx_p">To establish a human baseline, we recruit 20 native graduate students (each paid with $15) to complete the Chinese <span id="S4.SS1.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="S4.SS1.p3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span> together. No extra tutorials or examples are provided to ensure a fair comparison. We directly use this result as human performance since studies have found that cultural and language differences do not significantly affect ToM task performance across native-English and native-Chinese speakers <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib12" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bradford et al. (2018)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>

<td id="S4.T3.2.1.23.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_r" style="padding:-0.5pt 5.1pt;"><span id="S4.T3.2.1.23.3.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#007EDB;">73.2</span></td>
<td id="S4.T3.2.1.23.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="padding:-0.5pt 5.1pt;"><span id="S4.T3.2.1.23.4.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#007EDB;">71.2</span></td>

<td id="S4.T3.2.1.23.14" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F2F2F2;padding:-0.5pt 5.1pt;"><span id="S4.T3.2.1.23.14.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F2F2F2;">74.2</span></td>
<td id="S4.T3.2.1.23.15" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F2F2F2;padding:-0.5pt 5.1pt;"><span id="S4.T3.2.1.23.15.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#007EDB;--ltx-bg-color:#F2F2F2;">73.6</span></td></tr>
<tr id="S4.T3.2.1.24" class="ltx_tr">

<td id="S4.T3.2.1.24.9" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_r ltx_border_t" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F2F2F2;padding:-0.5pt 5.1pt;"><span id="S4.T3.2.1.24.9.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F2F2F2;">34.0</span></td>
<td id="S4.T3.2.1.24.10" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F2F2F2;padding:-0.5pt 5.1pt;"><span id="S4.T3.2.1.24.10.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F2F2F2;">60.8</span></td>
<td id="S4.T3.2.1.24.11" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_r ltx_border_t" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F2F2F2;padding:-0.5pt 5.1pt;"><span id="S4.T3.2.1.24.11.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F2F2F2;">58.0</span></td>
<td id="S4.T3.2.1.24.12" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_t" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F2F2F2;padding:-0.5pt 5.1pt;"><span id="S4.T3.2.1.24.12.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F2F2F2;">60.8</span></td>
<td id="S4.T3.2.1.24.13" class="ltx_td ltx_align_right ltx_border_t" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F2F2F2;padding:-0.5pt 5.1pt;"><span id="S4.T3.2.1.24.13.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F2F2F2;">61.9  <span class="ltx_rule" style="width:0.8pt;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"> </span></span></td>

<tr id="S4.T3.2.1.25" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="S4.T3.2.1.25.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_border_bb" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F2F2F2;padding:-0.5pt 5.1pt;"><span id="S4.T3.2.1.25.1.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F2F2F2;">LLM Grand Mean + CoT  <span class="ltx_rule" style="width:0.8pt;--ltx-bg-color:black;display:inline-block;"> </span></span></td>
<td id="S4.T3.2.1.25.2" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F2F2F2;padding:-0.5pt 5.1pt;"><span id="S4.T3.2.1.25.2.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F2F2F2;">59.9</span></td>
<td id="S4.T3.2.1.25.3" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_r" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F2F2F2;padding:-0.5pt 5.1pt;"><span id="S4.T3.2.1.25.3.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F2F2F2;">59.2</span></td>
<td id="S4.T3.2.1.25.4" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F2F2F2;padding:-0.5pt 5.1pt;"><span id="S4.T3.2.1.25.4.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F2F2F2;">53.4</span></td>
<td id="S4.T3.2.1.25.5" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb ltx_border_r" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F2F2F2;padding:-0.5pt 5.1pt;"><span id="S4.T3.2.1.25.5.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F2F2F2;">50.0</span></td>
<td id="S4.T3.2.1.25.6" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F2F2F2;padding:-0.5pt 5.1pt;"><span id="S4.T3.2.1.25.6.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F2F2F2;">60.5</span></td>

<td id="S4.T3.2.1.25.8" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_border_bb" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F2F2F2;padding:-0.5pt 5.1pt;"><span id="S4.T3.2.1.25.8.1" class="ltx_text" style="--ltx-bg-color:#F2F2F2;">40.7</span></td>

</span></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 3: </span>Ability-oriented ToM performance macro-averaged on 6 categories due to space limitation, while the complete results of all 31 abilities can be found in Appendix <a href="#A7" title="Appendix G Detailed Results of 31 Abilities ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G</span></a>, Table <a href="#A7.T21" title="Table 21 ‣ Appendix G Detailed Results of 31 Abilities ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">21</span></a>. </figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.2 </span>Main Results</h3>

<div id="S4.SS2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We show the ToM performance of LLMs across 8 tasks (Table <a href="#S3.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 3.3 Data Validation &amp; Translation ‣ 3 TMBench Construction ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>) and 6 ability categories (Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>), with detailed results on the 31 specific abilities presented in Appendix <a href="#A7" title="Appendix G Detailed Results of 31 Abilities ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G</span></a>. We now dissect the results and highlight several critical observations.</p>
</div>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Human vs. LLMs</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The average ToM performances of all LLMs are significantly lower than that of humans, with the smallest gap being 10.1% in task view (Human 85.4% vs. GPT-4-1106 75.3%) and 10.8% (Human 86.1% vs. GPT-4-0613 + CoT 75.3%) in ability view, respectively. Interestingly, in the false belief task (<span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_blackboard">𝔽𝔹𝕋</span>), LLMs like GPT-4-1106 even outperform humans, which we believe is explainable. In existing ToM inventories, there are relatively abundant samples for <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_blackboard">𝔽𝔹𝕋</span>, such as the Sally-Anne <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib6" title="" class="ltx_ref">Baron-Cohen et al. (1985)</a></cite> and Smarties <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wimmer and Perner (1983)</a></cite> tests. Moreover, the stories used in <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_blackboard">𝔽𝔹𝕋</span> are strictly templated, which further benefits LLMs’ generalization after being trained on existing samples. For example, they often involve PersonA moving something to a new location without PersonB knowing, and then asking about PersonB’s belief. It’s normal for LLMs to surpass humans in specific tasks and abilities, but this shouldn’t lead us to conclude that LLMs possess a human-level ToM. Instead, we should consider a general and robust ToM across tasks and abilities as the criterion for assessment.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">LLMs’ ToM Performance</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">GPT-4 series stands out with superior results in LLMs, and surpasses the second-tier GPT-3.5-Turbo series by over 10% points.
Among the open LLMs, Qwen-14B-Chat impressively outperforms other LLMs and even closely matches GPT-3.5-Turbo. Mistral-7B is also notable, not only surpassing ChatGLM3-6B but even outperforming LLaMA2-13B-Chat and Baichuan2-13B-Chat.
The MoE-type Mixtral-8x7B
does not outperform Mistral-7B, which contrasts to its task-solving performance and also underscores the unique nature of ToM evaluation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Vanilla vs. CoT Prompting</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Both task- and ability-oriented results indicate that CoT prompting almost never improves ToM performance and can even lead to declines. We believe CoT reasoning primarily serves to provide intrinsic context, breaking down complex tasks into simpler ones. However, if an LLM inherently lacks a robust ToM, its CoT decomposition process may struggle to align with genuine human cognitive reasoning, thereby failing to boost performance. We present a failure case of CoT prompting in Appendix <a href="#A9" title="Appendix I Case Study for CoT Prompting ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">I</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Differences Across ToM Tasks</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In Table <a href="#S3.T2" title="Table 2 ‣ 3.3 Data Validation &amp; Translation ‣ 3 TMBench Construction ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">2</span></a>, we calculate the “Grand Mean” performance of all LLMs on specific tasks. Notably, the faux-pas recognition test (<span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_blackboard">𝔽ℝ𝕋</span>) shows relatively high accuracy, partly because <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_blackboard">𝔽ℝ𝕋</span> includes a notable number of True/False questions, reducing its difficulty. The unexpected outcome test (<span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_blackboard">𝕌𝕆𝕋</span>) follows, mainly because a substantial portion of <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_blackboard">𝕌𝕆𝕋</span> involves direct emotion understanding tasks, a domain where NLP has abundant datasets, thus LLMs perform well. The poorest performance is observed in the scalar implicature task (<span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_blackboard">𝕊𝕀𝕋</span>), which requires understanding a character’s grasp of information based on quantifiers, involving mathematical reasoning where LLMs are typically weak. The persuasion story task (<span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px4.p1.1.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_blackboard">ℙ𝕊𝕋</span>) also proves challenging, focusing on the complex psychological activities of characters persuading others and requiring a comprehensive understanding of social contexts.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Differences Across ToM Abilities</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Further exploring Table <a href="#S4.T3" title="Table 3 ‣ 4.1 Experimental Setup ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">3</span></a>, the best-performing ability dimensions are <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Non-literal Communication</span> (overlaps with <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_blackboard">𝔽ℝ𝕋</span>) and <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Emotion</span>, consistent with the task-oriented results. The weakest category is <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.4" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Knowledge</span> (overlaps with <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_blackboard">𝕊𝕀𝕋</span>)—not referring to the LLMs’ own knowledge but testing whether LLMs understand the information propagation between characters in stories, which LLMs often struggle with. In Appendix <a href="#A7" title="Appendix G Detailed Results of 31 Abilities ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">G</span></a>, we delve deeper into LLMs’ performance across the 31 abilities.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px6" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">The Necessity of Bilingual Inventory</h4>

<div id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The averaged results show LLMs performing similarly in Chinese and English,
but this does not imply that LLMs perform identically in both languages. To assess the significance of any differences, we first conduct a Kolmogorov-Smirnov Test <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib2" title="" class="ltx_ref">AN (1933)</a></cite> on Chinese and English results, finding that neither task-oriented nor ability-oriented results follow a normal distribution (<span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">p</span>&lt;0.01). Thus, we employ the Wilcoxon Signed-Rank Test <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib69" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wilcoxon (1947)</a></cite> to examine the differences caused by languages, yielding <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">p</span>=0.019 (task) and <span id="S4.SS2.SSS0.Px6.p1.1.3" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">p</span>=0.016 (ability), both below the significance threshold of 0.05. Obviously, although the bilingual data are generated through translation with minimal semantic differences, LLMs exhibit significant performance discrepancies between Chinese and English contexts.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3" class="ltx_subsection">
<h3 class="ltx_title ltx_title_subsection"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_subsection">4.3 </span>In-Depth Analysis</h3>

<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">A Harder Coherent Test for LLMs</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">When evaluating task-oriented ToM performance, we use the simple average accuracy across all questions at that time. In fact, for all ToM tasks except <span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_blackboard">ℙ𝕊𝕋</span>, most stories are associated with multiple coherent questions probing different aspects of the social scenario within the story. A common and intuitive perspective is that for a story, subjects need to answer all coherent questions correctly to demonstrate a complete understanding <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al. (2023)</a></cite>, rather than just making educated guesses. Therefore, we further design a more challenging story-level coherent test for evaluation, where an LLM is considered to have failed a story if it incorrectly answers any question associated with that story.</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F4" class="ltx_figure"><object type="image/svg+xml" data="2402.15052v1/coherent.svg" id="S4.F4.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:229/172;" width="229" height="172"></object>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 4: </span>
The performance variance under the coherent test. Full results are present in Appendix <a href="#A8" title="Appendix H Detailed Results of Coherent Tests ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">H</span></a>, Table <a href="#A8.T22" title="Table 22 ‣ Appendix H Detailed Results of Coherent Tests ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">22</span></a>.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px1.p2.1" class="ltx_p">We present the average performance variation of all LLMs in Figure <a href="#S4.F4" title="Figure 4 ‣ A Harder Coherent Test for LLMs ‣ 4.3 In-Depth Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>. Under the coherent test, the ToM performance of all LLMs drops dramatically by at least 20% points, while humans only experience a decrease of 13.6% points. This widens the performance gap between the top-performing LLMs and humans from the original 10.1% to 16.2%, highlighting LLMs’ limitations in fully comprehending social scenarios like humans.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">LLMs Fail on Trivial ToM Questions</h4>

<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We now delve into an ability where LLMs perform particularly poorly: <span id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Knowledge/Knowledge-Pretend Links</span>. It’s important to note that this deliberate selection does not introduce bias against LLMs because, methodologically, failing even one ToM task implies the absence of a general ToM ability <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shapira et al. (2023)</a></cite>. Specifically, this ability tests whether subjects can understand that a person or object cannot imitate something they are unaware of.
This task is intuitive and straightforward for humans (achieving 93.3% accuracy) but proves difficult for LLMs. GPT-4-1106 and GPT-4-0613 achieve only 26.7% and 3.3% accuracy on English samples, respectively, which is nearly equivalent to or even worse than random guessing (full results can be found in Table <a href="#A7.T21" title="Table 21 ‣ Appendix G Detailed Results of 31 Abilities ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">21</span></a>).</p>
</div>
<figure id="S4.F5" class="ltx_figure"><img src="2402.15052v1/attention.png" id="S4.F5.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_landscape" style="aspect-ratio:229/162;" width="229" height="162" alt="Refer to caption">
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 5: </span>
The difference between the human and LLM’s attentions. Color intensity denotes attention weights.</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S4.SS3.SSS0.Px2.p2.1" class="ltx_p">To understand the reasons behind this poor performance, in Figure <a href="#S4.F5" title="Figure 5 ‣ LLMs Fail on Trivial ToM Questions ‣ 4.3 In-Depth Analysis ‣ 4 Experiments ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>, we visualize the decision-making process of an open LLM, ChatGLM3-6B, of which the weights are accessible. Specifically, when ChatGLM3-6B generates an incorrect option A, we average the attention scores across the attention heads in 20 layers, identifying the top-10 keywords that ChatGLM3-6B focuses on when answering the question. Clearly, LLMs still rely on semantic associations to answer ToM questions, aligning with previous research on LLMs’ illusory theory of mind <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al. (2023)</a></cite>.
For comparison, we also ask a student to provide the top-10 keywords. The results show that the student could correctly answer the question after reading only half of the story, further emphasizing the distinction between human and LLMs in ToM capabilities.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
</section>
<section id="S5" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">5 </span>Related Work</h2>

<div id="S5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">As LLMs have reached and sometimes even surpassed human performance in task solving, researchers have started to explore whether LLMs possess a ToM and exhibit human-like social intelligence. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib56" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sap et al. (2022)</a></cite> tested GPT-3 with SocialIQA <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib57" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sap et al. (2019)</a></cite> and ToMi <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib39" title="" class="ltx_ref">Le et al. (2019)</a></cite>, finding its performance significantly lower than humans. However, when it comes to instruction-tuned davince-002/003, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib37" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kosinski (2023)</a></cite> reported their performance as comparable to children aged 7 and 10, respectively, according to the experiments on 40 samples testing false beliefs. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib14" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bubeck et al. (2023)</a></cite> discovered that GPT-4 achieved impressive results on the Sally-Anne test with 10 samples. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib67" title="" class="ltx_ref">van Duijn et al. (2023)</a></cite> found that GPT-3.5/4 outperformed students aged 7 to 10 on various early inventories. This sparked some discussions about the “<span id="S5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">theory of mind may have spontaneously emerged in large language models</span>.”</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p2.1" class="ltx_p">However, opposing views emerged quickly. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib66" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ullman (2023)</a></cite> and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib58" title="" class="ltx_ref">Shapira et al. (2023)</a></cite> showed that trivial alterations to test samples could drastically decrease LLM’s ToM performance, highlighting their reliance on spurious correlations. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib30" title="" class="ltx_ref">Jones et al. (2023)</a></cite> found poor performance on tasks like scalar implicature, while <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib41" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al. (2023a)</a></cite>, <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib72" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wu et al. (2023)</a></cite>, and <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib32" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kim et al. (2023)</a></cite> observed limited abilities in reconstructed/high-order/conversational false belief tests, respectively. The debate on whether LLMs possess ToM underscores the need for a holistic benchmark. <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_citet"><a href="#bib.bib42" title="" class="ltx_ref">Ma et al. (2023b)</a></cite> made an inspiring attempt by testing about 9 ToM abilities of simulated geometric bodies in virtual 2D grids, but this setting cannot reflect human activities in real-world social scenarios.</p>
</div>
<div id="S5.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S5.p3.1" class="ltx_p">Different from existing ToM assessments for LLMs, our <span id="S5.p3.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="S5.p3.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span> includes 8 tasks and 31 abilities, comprising 2,860 multi-choice questions built from scratch and covering diverse real-world social scenarios. <span id="S5.p3.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="S5.p3.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span> establishes a systematic, automated, and original ToM benchmark that can continuously contribute to future research.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="S6" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_section">6 </span>Conclusions</h2>

<div id="S6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="S6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We introduce <span id="S6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="S6.p1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span>, the first systematic ToM benchmark for LLMs with an MCQ-type inventory entirely built from scratch.
We reveal that even the most advanced LLMs significantly lag behind human performance in ToM. Further in-depth analysis indicates that LLMs still struggle to comprehensively understand social scenarios, and tend to rely on semantic associations rather than human-like cognitive processes when addressing ToM questions.
By proposing <span id="S6.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="S6.p1.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span>, we aim to provide an effective and efficient platform for evaluating the ToM capabilities of LLMs and spur further research into LLMs that innately understand ToM, thereby improving how artificial intelligence can serve us in a human-friendly way.</p>
</div>
<div class="ltx_pagination ltx_role_newpage"></div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Limitations</h2>

<div id="Sx1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We discuss the limitations of our work as follows.</p>
</div>
<section id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Evaluation Protocol</h4>

<div id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In <span id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span>, we aim to cover a broad range of well-defined ToM tasks frequently used in psychology. It is important to recognize that additional ToM tasks exist, such as the imposing memory task <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib33" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kinderman et al. (1998)</a></cite>, which introduces unique evaluation protocols. Additionally, <span id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span> includes 31 abilities from the ATOMS framework that can be evaluated through textual modality. However, visual ToM tests are also classic and common in psychology, such as visual perspective taking - acknowledging that others have different visual percepts and adopting the visual perspective of another person. As multimodal LLMs like GPT-4V rapidly develop, ToM evaluations based on images and videos will also be applicable for LLMs. We advocate for future research to broaden the range of ToM assessments for LLMs, covering more tasks and abilities for a thorough evaluation.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Inventory Size</h4>

<div id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Due to the difficulty and cost of manual construction, although <span id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span> contains a total of 2,860 samples, the minimum number for some abilities is only 20. This may lead to inadequate testing of specific abilities. There is an opportunity for future work to expand the sample size, allowing for a more detailed and accurate analysis of each ability.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Inventory Languages</h4>

<div id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span> currently supports Chinese and English evaluation, where the Chinese data is originally created and the English data is obtained via translation. Although we have carefully designed the prompt for GPT-4 to complete the translation and manually reviewed all data, some cultural differences may still exist, e.g. fictitious person names, fictitious location names, etc. Future efforts could focus on localizing evaluation content and expanding language coverage to better reflect diverse cultural contexts.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">LLMs and Prompting Methods</h4>

<div id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In the experiments, we evaluate 10 popular representative LLMs, though additional LLMs could be included in future analyses. We use vanilla and CoT prompting methods for evaluation, while the recently emerging prompting methods such as “perspective taking” <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib70" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wilf et al. (2023)</a></cite> and “foresee and reflect” <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib74" title="" class="ltx_ref">Zhou et al. (2023)</a></cite> could also be explored to enhance the LLMs’ ToM performance.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">ToM Understanding vs. Application</h4>

<div id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">Our examination of LLMs’ ToM capabilities in <span id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span> is conducted by posing ToM-related questions and evaluating the responses. It’s crucial to note that an LLM’s intrinsic awareness of ToM principles does not necessarily translate to effective extrinsic ToM performance in human-AI interactions. These aspects represent progressive steps—from understanding to application. While <span id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1.2" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="Sx1.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.g2" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span> aims to address the foundational aspect, future research could explore more complex interactions, e.g., considering LLMs as autonomous social agents and assessing their dynamic ToM abilities in customized social scenarios.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="Sx2" class="ltx_section">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_section">Ethical Considerations</h2>

<div id="Sx2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We here elaborate on the potential ethical issues.</p>
</div>
<section id="Sx2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">ToM and Anthropomorphism</h4>

<div id="Sx2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">The theory of mind is a unique social cognitive ability inherent to humans. Evaluating LLMs’ ToM capabilities through <span id="Sx2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="Sx2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span> might lead to anthropomorphic interpretations, where LLMs are ascribed to human-like mental states. However, it’s crucial to clarify that our intention is not to humanize LLMs. Instead, we aim to enhance LLMs’ ability to understand and interpret human mental states and cognitive processes, thereby improving human-machine interaction. This endeavor is about bridging the communication gap, not erasing the fundamental differences between humans and machines.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx2.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Content Safety</h4>

<div id="Sx2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We authors have undergone professional training in psychology to understand ToM and reviewed broad psychological literature related to the tasks and abilities. We ensure that all test samples in <span id="Sx2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="Sx2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span> are free from unsafe, toxic, biased, and offensive content. All social scenarios in test stories are fictitious and do not involve any specific countries, locations, events, characters, or other identifiable information.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="Sx2.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Human Baseline</h4>

<div id="Sx2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="Sx2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">To establish the human baseline for <span id="Sx2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="Sx2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span>, we recruit graduate students who are native speakers of Chinese. This decision is made based on objective conditions available to us and does not reflect any intention of bias or unfairness towards individuals of any race, nationality, or other personal characteristics. Participants are selected based on the order of registration and get paid timely after the experiment. Participants complete experiments in an online document without providing any sensitive or personal information.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>

<section id="A1" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix A </span>Inventory Contamination in LLMs</h2>

<div id="A1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A1.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We use the Sally-Anne Test, a commonly applied false belief task, as a simple yet general example for observation. As shown in Table <a href="#A1.T4" title="Table 4 ‣ Appendix A Inventory Contamination in LLMs ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">4</span></a>, when prompted with the Sally-Anne Test scenarios, GPT-3.5-Turbo and GPT-4 can generate test samples that closely match the original examples, highlighting the potential risk of contamination in LLMs. For more inspection methods to identify contamination, please refer to related literature on this subject <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib23" title="" class="ltx_ref">Golchin and Surdeanu (2023)</a>; <a href="#bib.bib40" title="" class="ltx_ref">Li and Flanigan (2023)</a></cite>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A1.T4" class="ltx_table">
<table id="A1.T4.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="A1.T4.2.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A1.T4.2.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_center ltx_align_middle ltx_border_l ltx_border_r ltx_border_t" style="padding:0.5pt 2.8pt;"><span id="A1.T4.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Ground-Truth Sample in Sally-Anne Test</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A1.T4.2.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A1.T4.2.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_middle ltx_border_l ltx_border_r ltx_border_t" style="padding:0.5pt 2.8pt;">
<span id="A1.T4.2.2.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_middle" style="width:340.2pt;">
<span id="A1.T4.2.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">Sally first placed a marble into her basket. Then she left the scene, and the marble was transferred by Anne and hidden in her box. Then, when Sally returned, the experimenter asked the critical Belief Question: “Where will Sally look for her marble?”. The answer is “basket”.</span>
</span></td></tr>
