<td id="A1.T4.2.10.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_middle ltx_border_l ltx_border_r" style="padding:0.5pt 2.8pt;">
<span id="A1.T4.2.10.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_middle" style="width:340.2pt;">
<span id="A1.T4.2.10.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">Sally has a basket. Anne has a box. Sally puts a marble into her basket and then leaves to go for a walk. While Sally is away, Anne takes the marble from the basket and puts it into her box. Sally comes back.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A1.T4.2.11" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A1.T4.2.11.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_middle ltx_border_l ltx_border_r" style="padding:0.5pt 2.8pt;">
<span id="A1.T4.2.11.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_middle" style="width:340.2pt;">
<span id="A1.T4.2.11.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.T4.2.11.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Question</span>: Where will Sally look for her marble?</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A1.T4.2.12" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A1.T4.2.12.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_middle ltx_border_b ltx_border_l ltx_border_r" style="padding:0.5pt 2.8pt;">
<span id="A1.T4.2.12.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_middle" style="width:340.2pt;">
<span id="A1.T4.2.12.1.1.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A1.T4.2.12.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Answer</span>: Sally will look for her marble in the basket.</span>
</span></td></tr>
</table>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 4: </span>A case of contamination in LLMs for the frequently used Sally-Anne Test.</figcaption>
</figure>
</section>
<section id="A2" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix B </span>Details of Theory-of-Mind Tasks</h2>

<div id="A2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In <span id="A2.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="A2.p1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span>, we identify 8 social cognitive tasks from a broad view of psychology literature for ToM Evaluation.</p>
</div>
<section id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px1" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Unexpected Outcome Test</h4>

<div id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px1.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib21" title="" class="ltx_ref">Dyck et al. (2001)</a></cite> evaluates participants’ ability to infer characters’ mental states in scenarios with apparent discrepancies between emotion-eliciting contexts and the emotions actually elicited. Example data is present in Table <a href="#A3.T5" title="Table 5 ‣ Appendix C Details of Theory-of-Mind Abilities ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">5</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px2" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Scalar Implicature Task</h4>

<div id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px2.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib24" title="" class="ltx_ref">Goodman and Stuhlmüller (2013)</a></cite> involves scenarios where a speaker uses terms like “some” to imply “not all” in situations of incomplete information. It tests participants’ ability to infer meanings beyond literal expressions in conversational contexts. Example data is present in Table <a href="#A3.T6" title="Table 6 ‣ Appendix C Details of Theory-of-Mind Abilities ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px3" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Persuasion Story Task</h4>

<div id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px3.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib36" title="" class="ltx_ref">Kołodziejczyk and Bosacki (2016)</a></cite> assesses participants’ ability to understand and choose effective persuasion strategies, reflecting their understanding of how to influence others’ mental states and attitudes. Example data is present in Table <a href="#A3.T7" title="Table 7 ‣ Appendix C Details of Theory-of-Mind Abilities ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">7</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px4" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">False Belief Task</h4>

<div id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px4.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wimmer and Perner (1983)</a></cite> examines whether participants can distinguish between their own beliefs (true beliefs) and others’ beliefs (false beliefs) when they differ. Example data is present in Table <a href="#A3.T8" title="Table 8 ‣ Appendix C Details of Theory-of-Mind Abilities ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">8</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px5" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Ambiguous Story Task</h4>

<div id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px5.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib11" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bosacki and Wilde Astington (1999)</a></cite> presents ambiguous social vignettes, followed by questions that gauge participants’ understanding of others’ mental states, like emotions and beliefs, in uncertain situations. Example data is present in Table <a href="#A3.T9" title="Table 9 ‣ Appendix C Details of Theory-of-Mind Abilities ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">9</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px6" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Hinting Test</h4>

<div id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px6.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib18" title="" class="ltx_ref">Corcoran et al. (1995)</a></cite> assesses participants’ ability to infer mental states from indirect hints in social interactions, reflecting their understanding of implied meanings beyond literal statements. Example data is present in Table <a href="#A3.T10" title="Table 10 ‣ Appendix C Details of Theory-of-Mind Abilities ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">10</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px7" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Strange Story Task</h4>

<div id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px7.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Happé (1994)</a></cite> requires participants to infer characters’ mental states in stories that include complex social communications such as lies, white lies, misunderstandings, persuasion, irony, contrary emotions, jokes, double bluffs, pretense, figures of speech, forgetting, and appearance versus reality. Example data is present in Table <a href="#A3.T11" title="Table 11 ‣ Appendix C Details of Theory-of-Mind Abilities ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">11</span></a> (part1) and Table <a href="#A3.T12" title="Table 12 ‣ Appendix C Details of Theory-of-Mind Abilities ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">12</span></a> (part2).</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px8" class="ltx_paragraph">
<h4 class="ltx_title ltx_title_paragraph">Faux-pas Recognition Test</h4>

<div id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A2.SS0.SSS0.Px8.p1.1" class="ltx_p"><cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib7" title="" class="ltx_ref">Baron-Cohen et al. (1999)</a></cite> tests participants’ ability to recognize when characters in social stories commit a faux pas, reflecting their understanding of social norms and others’ perspectives. Example data is present in Table <a href="#A3.T13" title="Table 13 ‣ Appendix C Details of Theory-of-Mind Abilities ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">13</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
</section>
<section id="A3" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix C </span>Details of Theory-of-Mind Abilities</h2>

<div id="A3.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In <span id="A3.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="A3.p1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span>, we further identify 31 social cognitive abilities in 6 dimensions according to the ATOMS <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib8" title="" class="ltx_ref">Beaudoin et al. (2020)</a></cite> framework in psychology for ToM Evaluation.
Among them, 19 abilities are included in previous tasks, and example data can be found from the corresponding tasks. Additionally, we have constructed extra test data for the rest 12 abilities, and example data can be found in Table <a href="#A3.T14" title="Table 14 ‣ Appendix C Details of Theory-of-Mind Abilities ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">14</span></a> (Emotion), Table <a href="#A3.T15" title="Table 15 ‣ Appendix C Details of Theory-of-Mind Abilities ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">15</span></a> (Desire), Table <a href="#A3.T16" title="Table 16 ‣ Appendix C Details of Theory-of-Mind Abilities ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">16</span></a> (Intention), and Table <a href="#A3.T17" title="Table 17 ‣ Appendix C Details of Theory-of-Mind Abilities ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">17</span></a> (Knowledge).</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p2" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p2.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.p2.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Emotion</span> involves the abilities to understand that situational factors influence people’s emotional states, that people can experience complex emotions, and that people can regulate emotional expressions.
This dimension encompasses 7 abilities.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p3" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p3.1" class="ltx_p">(I) Typical emotional reactions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib35" title="" class="ltx_ref">Knafo et al. (2009)</a></cite>: Inferring a person’s emotional reactions based on situations that typically elicit certain emotions/inferring a preceding event based on a person’s emotional reaction.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p4" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p4.1" class="ltx_p">(II) Atypical emotional reactions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib20" title="" class="ltx_ref">Denham (1986)</a></cite>: Inferring or explaining a person’s emotional reactions based on situations eliciting emotions that are atypical compared to what is usually expected.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p5" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p5.1" class="ltx_p">(III) Discrepant emotions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib10" title="" class="ltx_ref">Borke (1971)</a></cite>: Understanding that people may have discrepant feelings about an event.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p6" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p6.1" class="ltx_p">(IV) Mixed emotions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib25" title="" class="ltx_ref">Gordis et al. (1989)</a></cite>: Understanding that people may feel mixed emotions or different emotions successively.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p7" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p7.1" class="ltx_p">(V) Hidden emotions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib27" title="" class="ltx_ref">Harris et al. (1986)</a></cite>: Understanding that other people may hide their emotions.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p8" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p8.1" class="ltx_p">(VI) Moral emotions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pons and Harris (2000)</a></cite>: Understanding that negative feelings might arise following a reprehensible action.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p9" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p9.1" class="ltx_p">(VII) Emotion regulation <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib52" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pons and Harris (2000)</a></cite>: Understanding that others might use strategies to regulate their emotions.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p10" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p10.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.p10.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Desire</span> involves the abilities to understand that people have subjective desires, preferences, and wants that influence their emotions and actions.
This dimension encompasses 4 abilities.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p11" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p11.1" class="ltx_p">(I) Discrepant desires <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib55" title="" class="ltx_ref">Repacholi and Gopnik (1997)</a></cite>: Understanding that different people may have discrepant desires.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p12" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p12.1" class="ltx_p">(II) Multiple desires <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib9" title="" class="ltx_ref">Bennett and Galpert (1993)</a></cite>: Understanding the co-existence of multiple desires simultaneously or successively in one person.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p13" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p13.1" class="ltx_p">(III) Desires influence on emotions and actions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib68" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wellman and Bartsch (1988)</a></cite>: Understanding that people’s emotions and actions are influenced by their desires/preferences.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p14" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p14.1" class="ltx_p">(IV) Desire-action contradiction <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib17" title="" class="ltx_ref">Colonnesi et al. (2008)</a></cite>: Producing plausible explanations when actions contradict stated desires/preferences.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p15" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p15.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.p15.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Intention</span> involves the abilities to understand that people undertake actions in pursuit of goals and intentions.
This dimension encompasses 4 abilities.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p16" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p16.1" class="ltx_p">(I) Completion of failed actions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib43" title="" class="ltx_ref">Meltzoff (1995)</a></cite>: Understanding another person’s intent, as demonstrated by completing their failed action.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p17" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p17.1" class="ltx_p">(II) Discrepant intentions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib31" title="" class="ltx_ref">Killen et al. (2011)</a></cite>: Understanding that identical actions/results can be achieved with different intentions.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p18" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p18.1" class="ltx_p">(III) Prediction of actions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib50" title="" class="ltx_ref">Phillips et al. (2002)</a></cite>: Predicting people’s actions based on their intentions.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p19" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p19.1" class="ltx_p">(IV) Intentions explanations <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib61" title="" class="ltx_ref">Smiley (2001)</a></cite>: Producing plausible intention explanations for different types of observed social events.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p20" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p20.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.p20.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Knowledge</span> involves the abilities to understand that others have access to different knowledge based on their perceptions, information they have received, or familiarity with things.
This dimension encompasses 4 abilities.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p21" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p21.1" class="ltx_p">(I) Knowledge-pretend play links <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib3" title="" class="ltx_ref">Aronson and Golomb (1999)</a></cite>: Understanding that someone who does not know something exists cannot engage in “pretend play” that incorporates that knowledge.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p22" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p22.1" class="ltx_p">(II) Percepts-knowledge links <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib51" title="" class="ltx_ref">Pillow (1989)</a></cite>: Understanding that someone who does not have access to perceptual information (i.e., by looking, hearing, etc.) may not have access to knowledge.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p23" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p23.1" class="ltx_p">(III) Information-knowledge links <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib49" title="" class="ltx_ref">Peskin et al. (2014)</a></cite>: Understanding that someone who was not informed or is not familiar with something may not know.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p24" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p24.1" class="ltx_p">(IV) Knowledge-attention links <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib45" title="" class="ltx_ref">Moll et al. (2006)</a></cite>: Understanding that something new is more interesting to someone than something already known.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p25" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p25.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.p25.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Belief</span> involves the abilities to understand that people can hold beliefs about the world that are different from reality or different from one’s own beliefs.
This dimension encompasses 6 abilities</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p26" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p26.1" class="ltx_p">(I) Content false beliefs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib28" title="" class="ltx_ref">Hogrefe et al. (1986)</a></cite>: Familiar container with an unexpected content: Understanding the false belief held by someone who never opened the container.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p27" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p27.1" class="ltx_p">(II) Location false beliefs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib71" title="" class="ltx_ref">Wimmer and Perner (1983)</a></cite>: Understanding the false belief held by someone who did not witness or was not informed of a displacement or change of action.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p28" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p28.1" class="ltx_p">(III) Identity false beliefs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib22" title="" class="ltx_ref">Flavell et al. (1986)</a></cite>: Understanding that when something looks/sounds/smells like something else, a person may hold a false belief about its identity.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p29" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p29.1" class="ltx_p">(IV) Second-order beliefs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib48" title="" class="ltx_ref">Perner and Wimmer (1985)</a></cite>: Understanding the second-order belief or false belief held by someone who doe not know somebody else was informed (e.g., of a misleading identity, a misleading location, etc.).</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p30" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p30.1" class="ltx_p">(V) Beliefs based action/emotions <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib63" title="" class="ltx_ref">Swettenham (1996)</a></cite>: Predicting another emotions or actions based on their stated beliefs/Inferring another person’s belief based on their stated action or emotion.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p31" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p31.1" class="ltx_p">(VI) Sequence false beliefs <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib13" title="" class="ltx_ref">Brambring and Asbrock (2010)</a></cite>: Understanding the false belief created when a predictable sequence of stimuli is broken with the intrusion of an unexpected stimulus.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p32" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p32.1" class="ltx_p"><span id="A3.p32.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold">Non-literal Communication</span> involves the abilities to understand that communication can convey meaning beyond the literal words spoken.
This dimension encompasses 6 abilities.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p33" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p33.1" class="ltx_p">(I) Irony/sarcasm <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib62" title="" class="ltx_ref">Sullivan et al. (1995)</a></cite>: Understanding that other people may lie in order to be ironic/sarcastic.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p34" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p34.1" class="ltx_p">(II) Egocentric lies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Happé (1994)</a></cite>: Understanding that someone may consciously lie in order to avoid a problem or to get its way.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p35" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p35.1" class="ltx_p">(III) White lies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Happé (1994)</a></cite>: Understanding that someone may lie in order to spare another’s feelings.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p36" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p36.1" class="ltx_p">(IV) Involuntary lies <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Happé (1994)</a></cite>: Understanding that someone may tell a “lie” without knowing.</p>
</div>
<div id="A3.p37" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A3.p37.1" class="ltx_p">(V) Humor <cite class="ltx_cite ltx_citemacro_cite"><a href="#bib.bib26" title="" class="ltx_ref">Happé (1994)</a></cite>: Understanding that someone may tell a “lie” in order to make a joke.</p>

<section id="A4" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix D </span>Detailed Data Statistics</h2>

<div id="A4.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A4.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We present the detailed data statistics of 31 theory-of-mind abilities in Table <a href="#A4.T18" title="Table 18 ‣ Appendix D Detailed Data Statistics ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">18</span></a>. For each task, we collect <math id="A4.p1.m1" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\geq" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>≥</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\geq</annotation></semantics></math>100 samples, covering 19/31 abilities. Additionally, for the rest 12 abilities not covered in the 8 tasks, we further collect <math id="A4.p1.m2" class="ltx_Math" alttext="\geq" display="inline" intent=":literal"><semantics><mo>≥</mo><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\geq</annotation></semantics></math>20 extra samples per ability.</p>
</div>

<section id="A5" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix E </span>Prompts for Data Translation</h2>

<div id="A5.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A5.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We present the prompts for Chinese to English translation of <span id="A5.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="A5.p1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span> in Table <a href="#A5.T19" title="Table 19 ‣ Appendix E Prompts for Data Translation ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">19</span></a>.</p>
</div>
<figure id="A5.T19" class="ltx_table">
<table id="A5.T19.2" class="ltx_tabular ltx_centering ltx_align_middle">
<tr id="A5.T19.2.1" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A5.T19.2.1.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_middle ltx_border_l ltx_border_r ltx_border_tt" style="padding:0.5pt 2.8pt;">
<span id="A5.T19.2.1.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_middle" style="width:340.2pt;">
<span id="A5.T19.2.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">You are an experienced translator who only uses the *Present Tense* of English in translating all Chinese texts.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A5.T19.2.2" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A5.T19.2.2.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_middle ltx_border_l ltx_border_r" style="padding:0.5pt 2.8pt;"></td></tr>
<tr id="A5.T19.2.3" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A5.T19.2.3.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_middle ltx_border_l ltx_border_r" style="padding:0.5pt 2.8pt;">
<span id="A5.T19.2.3.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_middle" style="width:340.2pt;">
<span id="A5.T19.2.3.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">[Task]</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A5.T19.2.4" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A5.T19.2.4.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_middle ltx_border_l ltx_border_r" style="padding:0.5pt 2.8pt;">
<span id="A5.T19.2.4.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_middle" style="width:340.2pt;">
<span id="A5.T19.2.4.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">Translate the given Chinese text to English. You should strictly follow the below rules.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A5.T19.2.5" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A5.T19.2.5.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_middle ltx_border_l ltx_border_r" style="padding:0.5pt 2.8pt;">
<span id="A5.T19.2.5.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_middle" style="width:340.2pt;">
<span id="A5.T19.2.5.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">(1) You should use the high school-level vocabulary with frequently-used words.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A5.T19.2.6" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A5.T19.2.6.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_middle ltx_border_l ltx_border_r" style="padding:0.5pt 2.8pt;">
<span id="A5.T19.2.6.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_middle" style="width:340.2pt;">
<span id="A5.T19.2.6.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">(2) You should only present the translation results without any other explanations.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A5.T19.2.7" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A5.T19.2.7.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_middle ltx_border_l ltx_border_r" style="padding:0.5pt 2.8pt;">
<span id="A5.T19.2.7.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_middle" style="width:340.2pt;">
<span id="A5.T19.2.7.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">(3) The translation result must be in the present tense, do not use any other tenses, regardless of the text content.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A5.T19.2.8" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A5.T19.2.8.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_middle ltx_border_l ltx_border_r" style="padding:0.5pt 2.8pt;">
<span id="A5.T19.2.8.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_middle" style="width:340.2pt;">
<span id="A5.T19.2.8.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">(4) All verbs in the translation results should be in the present tense, e.g., you should use ‘is’ instead of ‘was’, ‘are’ instead of ‘were’, ‘give/gives instead of ‘gave’, ‘design/designs’ instead of ‘designed’, and et al.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A5.T19.2.9" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A5.T19.2.9.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_middle ltx_border_l ltx_border_r" style="padding:0.5pt 2.8pt;">
<span id="A5.T19.2.9.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_middle" style="width:340.2pt;">
<span id="A5.T19.2.9.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">(5) The given Chinese text in json format, with the keys being story, question, option_a, option_b, option_c and option_d. Please return the English translation in the original json format. Note that the above key remains unchanged, only translate their values.</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A5.T19.2.10" class="ltx_tr">
<td id="A5.T19.2.10.1" class="ltx_td ltx_align_left ltx_align_middle ltx_border_l ltx_border_r" style="padding:0.5pt 2.8pt;"></td></tr>

<span id="A5.T19.2.11.1.1" class="ltx_inline-block ltx_align_middle" style="width:340.2pt;">
<span id="A5.T19.2.11.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">[Input Chinese Text]:</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A5.T19.2.12" class="ltx_tr">

<span id="A5.T19.2.12.1.1.1" class="ltx_p">{<span id="A5.T19.2.12.1.1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">Chinese Sample</span>}</span>
</span></td></tr>
<tr id="A5.T19.2.13" class="ltx_tr">

<section id="A6" class="ltx_appendix">

<div id="A6.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A6.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We present the prompts for <span id="A6.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_smallcaps">T<img src="2402.15052v1/logo-noo.png" id="A6.p1.g1" class="ltx_graphics ltx_img_square" style="aspect-ratio:11/10;" width="11" height="10" alt="[Uncaptioned image]">MBench</span> evaluation in Table <a href="#A6.T20" title="Table 20 ‣ Appendix F Prompts for ToM Evaluation ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">20</span></a>.</p>

</table>
</span></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 21: </span>ToM performance for 31 specific abilities of all LLMs. The best results of vanilla prompting are in <span id="A7.T21.5" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#ED6498;">pink</span>, and those of CoT prompting are in <span id="A7.T21.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#007EDB;">blue</span>.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A7.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A7.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We present the detailed experimental results of 31 theory-of-mind abilities in Table <a href="#A7.T21" title="Table 21 ‣ Appendix G Detailed Results of 31 Abilities ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">21</span></a>. Overall, LLMs have not yet achieved a general and robust human-level ToM performance. The GPT-4 series shows the best performance in most specific abilities and even surpasses human performance in 9 out of 31 abilities. We attribute this to two main reasons: First, certain abilities, such as <span id="A7.p1.1.1" class="ltx_text ltx_font_italic">Emotion/Typical emotional reactions</span>, relate to samples that are quite direct and simple. LLMs have encountered many similar training datasets, thus achieving high accuracy. Second, limited by human resources, some abilities have a relatively small number of samples, insufficient to showcase the general advantage of humans over LLMs.</p>
</div>
</section>

</table>
</span></div>
<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_table">Table 22: </span>The ToM performance drop of all LLMs in the coherent test.
The best results of vanilla prompting in coherent tests are in <span id="A8.T22.6" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#ED6498;">pink</span>, and those of CoT prompting are in <span id="A8.T22.7" class="ltx_text ltx_font_bold" style="--ltx-fg-color:#007EDB;">blue</span>. No performance drop occurs in the persuasion story task since each story in <span id="A8.T22.8" class="ltx_text ltx_font_typewriter">PST</span> corresponds to only one question.
</figcaption>
</figure>
<div id="A8.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A8.p1.1" class="ltx_p">We present the detailed results of coherent tests on all LLMs with vanilla/CoT prompting in Table <a href="#A8.T22" title="Table 22 ‣ Appendix H Detailed Results of Coherent Tests ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">22</span></a>.</p>
</div>
</section>
<section id="A9" class="ltx_appendix">
<h2 class="ltx_title ltx_title_appendix"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_appendix">Appendix I </span>Case Study for CoT Prompting</h2>

<div id="A9.p1" class="ltx_para">
<p id="A9.p1.1" class="ltx_p">In Figure <a href="#A9.F6" title="Figure 6 ‣ Appendix I Case Study for CoT Prompting ‣ TMBench: Benchmarking Theory of Mind in Large Language Models" class="ltx_ref"><span class="ltx_text ltx_ref_tag">6</span></a>, we show a failed CoT reasoning process of GPT-4-0613. It’s evident that while LLMs can break down questions into detailed parts, they still struggle to provide the correct answer.</p>
</div>

<figcaption class="ltx_caption ltx_centering"><span class="ltx_tag ltx_tag_figure">Figure 6: </span>
A case of CoT prompting on GPT-4-0613.</figcaption>
